record.paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
record.original_question: If every graph has a three-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend cube-drawing of volume O(Δ^3 n), does it follow that every graph has a three-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend drawing of volume O(Δ^2 m), where m is the number of edges and Δ is the maximum degree?

evidence.quote: If the answer is yes, does every graph have a 1-bend drawing of volume O(∆2m)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ an axis-aligned box (a rectangular parallelepiped with integer corner coordinates and pairwise disjoint interiors) in $\mathbb{Z}^3$, and to each edge $uv\in E$ a path consisting of axis-parallel line segments whose endpoints lie on the boundaries of the boxes for $u$ and $v$, such that distinct edge routes intersect only at common endpoints, and an edge route does not intersect the interior of any box. Such a drawing is called a 1-bend drawing if every edge route consists of at most two axis-parallel segments (i.e., has at most one bend). The volume of a drawing is the volume of the smallest axis-aligned bounding box containing the entire drawing. A cube-drawing is one in which every vertex's box is a cube.

Let $\Delta$ denote the maximum degree, $n=|V|$, and $m=|E|$. 

Suppose it is true that every simple graph $G$ admits a 3-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend cube-drawing of volume $O(\Delta^3 n)$. Does it then follow that every simple graph $G$ admits a 3-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend drawing (with general box vertices) of volume $O(\Delta^2 m)$?
artifact.status_search_result: No source located in a brief search establishes a resolution of this conditional implication. The problem appears to remain unresolved (or at least not publicly settled), but this could not be verified definitively, so the status is recorded as unknown.
